profile.a: The author, writing individually for Business and Sustainable Development, as an outside adviser assessing BP.
BP's leadership, which has to decide whether to expand its electric vehicle (EV) charging network.
Whether BP should scale up EV charging and organise the move around four UN Sustainable Development Goals: 7 (clean energy), 9 (infrastructure), 12 (responsible production) and 13 (climate action).
Handed in on 12 November 2024. The decision looks ahead to 2030, when the UK requires 80% of new vehicles to be non-fossil and Shell aims to have 90% of drivers within 10 minutes of a rapid charger.
The UK, mainland Europe and North America, with offshore wind in Northern Europe as BP's main renewable base.

Transport produced 21.11% of global CO2 in 2023 and power 38.24%. BP has committed more than $69bn to the 2010 Gulf of Mexico spill and needs both a credible net-zero story and a business that survives falling fossil fuel demand.

Each SDG target is mapped to concrete actions, then four market forces (policy, EV demand, renewable supply, competition) are assessed for opportunity and risk, and Natura's Integral P&L, regeneration and the Corporate Knights ranking are proposed as ways to measure progress.

charts.title: Where global CO2 came from in 2023
charts.takeaway: Power and transport together produce nearly 60% of emissions. EV charging sits exactly where the two meet, which is why the paper picks it as BP's lever: clean charging cuts transport emissions only if the power behind it is also clean.
charts.source: Pages 6 and 9. 'All other sources' is the remainder of the two stated shares.

charts.title: How fast each part of the system has to grow
charts.takeaway: The paper's real constraint is supply, not demand. If renewable supply cannot grow about 20 times, the extra charging load is met by coal, gas or incineration and EVs lose most of their emissions advantage.
charts.source: Pages 9 and 10. The infrastructure figure is the paper's 'at least one order of magnitude'.

charts.title: The timeline the decision sits on

items.label: Gulf of Mexico spill: BP commits more than $69bn
UN adopts the Sustainable Development Goals
EV market starts a fourfold rise to 2025
Paper recommends BP scales up EV charging
UK: 80% of new vehicles non-fossil; Shell: 90% of drivers within 10 minutes

charts.takeaway: The window is short. Competitors and regulation converge on 2030, so the paper argues BP has to commit early to secure locations before the network is built by others.

charts.title: From each SDG target to a concrete action for BP

items.title: Clean energy (7.2, 7.3, 7.a)
items: Expand offshore wind in Northern Europe
Pair wind farms with hydrogen storage
Solar panels and batteries at charging stations

items.title: Infrastructure (9.1, 9.4)
items: Smart-grid charging timed to grid carbon intensity
Mobile charging vans for remote areas
AI app predicting queues and routes

items.title: Responsible production (12.6)
items: Shift investment to renewables
Gradually reduce oil and gas output
Carbon capture and storage

items.title: Climate action (13.2)
items: Rapid-charging hubs at existing petrol stations
Kerbside chargers with local authorities
Dynamic pricing to move charging off-peak

charts.takeaway: Every goal turns into actions BP can start with assets it already owns: petrol station sites, offshore wind and energy trading.

charts.title: The four forces: what helps and what threatens the investment

left.title: Opportunities
items: Policy: UK, US and EU mandates create guaranteed demand
Market: EV demand quadruples 2021-2025
Supply: BP can already connect renewables and co-locate solar at chargers
Competition: Shell's pace shows the market is real and can be matched

right.title: Risks
items: Policy: support changes with the ruling party (UK example)
Market: range anxiety, upfront cost and thin networks slow adoption
Supply: renewables must scale about 20x or emissions rise again
Competition: oversupply in some areas, undersupply in others, and a shortage of maintenance talent

charts.takeaway: The paper treats the risks as manageable but never prices them; the recommendation to scale up rests on the opportunities outweighing risks that remain unquantified.
